past_medical_history: Mild age-related white matter changes (noted on prior CT 3 years ago — reported as 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis')
family_history: Mother had memory problems in her 70s — unclear diagnosis
Father died of myocardial infarction at age 72

social_history.living_situation: Lives with husband; two adult children check in regularly

patient.chief_complaint: 18-month progressive difficulty walking, urinary urgency, and slowed thinking — referred for tap test evaluation
patient.history_present_illness: A 70-year-old right-handed retired schoolteacher with hypertension and diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus was admitted for inpatient tap trial evaluation after 18 months of progressive decline in gait, bladder control, and cognition. Her husband first noticed her gait change about 18 months ago — she began taking shorter steps, appeared to 'shuffle,' and her feet seemed to 'stick to the floor.' Over the next several months she had two near-falls and began using a cane. Gait symptoms are the most prominent and most distressing feature. Approximately 12 months ago she developed urinary urgency with occasional urge incontinence; she now wears a pad daily and has had nocturnal urgency waking her two to three times per week. Cognitive symptoms followed: her husband describes her as slower in conversation, repeating herself, and taking longer to manage finances and scheduling — tasks she previously performed effortlessly. She recalls her own cognition as 'slower, not forgetful.' MMSE obtained in the outpatient clinic was 25/30. Brain MRI ordered by her neurologist demonstrated ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.36, callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH pattern, and mild periventricular white matter hyperintensity; a prior CT scan 3 years ago had noted only 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis.' She was referred for inpatient tap trial. She denies headache, diplopia, nausea, limb weakness, tremor, or sensory symptoms. No history of head trauma, meningitis, or subarachnoid hemorrhage.

neurological_exam.mental_status: Alert, oriented x4. Speech is fluent but mildly slowed. No aphasia. MoCA 23/30 — loses 3 points on attention and trail-making, 2 on delayed recall, 1 on clock drawing. Frontal-subcortical pattern; episodic memory relatively preserved. No perseveration. Mild executive slowing on verbal fluency (9 words/min on phonemic task).
neurological_exam.cranial_nerves: Pupils equal and reactive, 3 mm bilaterally. Extraocular movements full, no nystagmus. No papilledema on fundoscopy. Facial sensation intact. Tongue midline.
neurological_exam.motor: Normal tone and strength throughout. No resting tremor. No cogwheel rigidity. No asterixis.
neurological_exam.sensory: Vibration mildly reduced at ankles bilaterally (age-appropriate). Pinprick and light touch intact throughout. Joint position sense intact at toes.
neurological_exam.reflexes: 2+ biceps and brachioradialis bilaterally. 2+ patellar bilaterally. 1+ Achilles bilaterally. Bilateral plantar flexors.
neurological_exam.coordination: Finger-nose intact bilaterally. Heel-shin mildly clumsy bilaterally.
neurological_exam.gait: Magnetic, broad-based, short-stepped gait with markedly reduced foot clearance. Freezing at initiation and at doorway threshold. En bloc turning requiring 7-8 steps. Unable to tandem walk. Uses cane. TUG 26 seconds. 10-meter walk 19 seconds. Pull test: 2 steps backward, recovers without falling.
neurological_exam.additional: Bilateral frontal release signs: grasp reflex present bilaterally. No cogwheel rigidity. No orthostatic hypotension on standing (BP 134/82 lying, 130/80 standing).

findings.location: bilateral lateral ventricles and third ventricle

signal_characteristics.description: Symmetrically enlarged bilateral lateral ventricles and mildly enlarged third ventricle; Evans index 0.36
Disproportionately enlarged subarachnoid spaces: narrowed high-convexity and medial parasagittal sulci contrasting with widened Sylvian fissures bilaterally — consistent with DESH morphology

findings.location: corpus callosum — coronal T1 section at posterior commissure level

signal_characteristics.description: Callosal angle 72 degrees on coronal T1 imaging
Thinning and mild upward bowing of the body of the corpus callosum on sagittal imaging
Periventricular FLAIR/T2 hyperintensity — thin rim capping the frontal and occipital horns, consistent with transependymal CSF seepage; mild scattered subcortical T2 foci also present
Prominent aqueductal flow void on sagittal T1 and T2 sequences
Mild-to-moderate bilateral periventricular and subcortical FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2); scattered subcortical foci in frontal and parietal regions; no confluent white matter disease

additional_observations: No intracranial mass, hemorrhage, extra-axial collection, or midline shift.
No evidence of obstructive hydrocephalus. Basal cisterns patent.
No restricted diffusion. No abnormal enhancement on post-contrast sequences.
Cortical sulcal atrophy is mild and is disproportionately less prominent than the degree of ventricular enlargement.
mri.impression: 1. Ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.36 and callosal angle 72 degrees. Ventricular enlargement is disproportionate to the mild degree of cortical sulcal atrophy. 2. DESH morphology: narrowed high-convexity sulci with widened Sylvian fissures. 3. Corpus callosum thinning and upward bowing. Prominent aqueductal flow void. Periventricular transependymal T2/FLAIR signal. 4. Mild-to-moderate periventricular and subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2); no confluent disease. 5. No mass, hemorrhage, or obstructive lesion

labs.interpretation: Fasting glucose mildly elevated at 108 mg/dL, consistent with known diet-controlled type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 6.4%, near-target). TSH, vitamin B12, folate, RPR, and HIV Ag/Ab all within normal limits. Remaining indices within normal limits.

csf.interpretation: Opening pressure: 13 cmH2O. WBC: 1 cell/mcL (lymphocyte). Protein: 41 mg/dL. Glucose: 68 mg/dL (ratio 0.63). No malignant cells. AD biomarkers: beta-amyloid-42 836 pg/mL (normal), total tau 184 pg/mL (normal), phospho-tau 24 pg/mL (normal). Large-volume tap performed: 40 mL removed. Pre-tap timed-up-and-go (TUG) 26 seconds; post-tap TUG at 2 hours 21 seconds (19% improvement); post-tap TUG at 24 hours 17 seconds (35% improvement). Pre-tap 10-meter walk 19 seconds; post-tap 10-meter walk at 24 hours 13 seconds (32% improvement). Pre-tap MoCA 23/30; post-tap MoCA at 24 hours 26/30 (3-point improvement). Gait description at 24 hours: improved step height and stride length, less freezing at initiation, turning in 4-5 steps (vs 7-8 pre-tap)

specialized_test.test_type: Neuropsychological battery — baseline evaluation prior to tap trial

findings.result: Moderately impaired — phonemic fluency 9 words/min (10th percentile); Trail Making Test Part B 142 seconds (below 10th percentile for age); Luria fist-edge-palm sequence impaired
Moderately impaired — Digit Symbol Coding 28 (12th percentile for age); WAIS-IV Processing Speed Index 78
Mildly impaired — Digit Span forward 6, backward 3 (18th percentile)
Mildly impaired — HVLT-R Delayed Recall 5/12 (22nd percentile); recognition memory relatively preserved (10/12 correct)
Within normal limits — Boston Naming Test 52/60; no paraphasias
Mildly impaired — Rey-Osterrieth Complex Figure copy 28/36 (20th percentile)

specialized_test.impression: Neuropsychological profile demonstrates prominent executive dysfunction and processing speed impairment, with mild deficits in working memory, episodic memory, and visuospatial function. Language is within normal limits. The pattern is consistent with a frontal-subcortical cognitive profile. Episodic memory recognition is relatively spared relative to recall, which is more consistent with a retrieval deficit than an encoding deficit

findings.result: Negative amyloid PET — CL score 8 (below threshold of 24.4)

output.impression: Negative — sparse-to-no amyloid neuritic plaque density. CL score 8, below the positivity threshold of 24.4
Markedly hyperdynamic aqueductal CSF flow. Peak velocity 24 cm/s (reference <18 cm/s); net stroke volume 88 mcL/cycle (reference <42 mcL/cycle). Both values exceed published normative ranges

output.test_type: Neuropsychological testing — post-tap reassessment (24 hours after 40 mL large-volume LP)

findings.pre_tap: Moderately impaired — phonemic fluency 9/min; TMT-B 142 sec
findings.post_tap: Mild improvement — phonemic fluency 12/min (33% improvement); TMT-B 118 sec (17% improvement)

output.impression: Post-tap reassessment at 24 hours demonstrates improvement in executive function and processing speed relative to baseline. Phonemic fluency improved from 9 to 12 words/min (33%); TMT-B improved from 142 to 118 seconds (17%); MoCA improved from 23 to 26 (3 points). Working memory and episodic memory showed modest improvement. The pattern of improvement is most pronounced in frontal-subcortical domains

findings.finding: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity — involuntary contractions at 140 mL fill
Reduced maximum cystometric capacity 260 mL (reference 400-500 mL)

output.impression: Neurogenic detrusor overactivity. Involuntary detrusor contractions at 140 mL fill; maximum cystometric capacity 260 mL. No urodynamic evidence of outlet obstruction. Pattern is consistent with detrusor overactivity of neurogenic origin

output.query: idiopathic normal pressure hydrocephalus diagnosis tap test shunt response predictors

results.finding: Relkin et al. (2005) INPH Study Group criteria define probable iNPH as chronic gait disturbance + ventriculomegaly (Evans index >0.3) without alternative cause + opening pressure ≤24.5 cmH2O. Gait disturbance is typically the earliest and most prominent symptom.

Tisell et al. (2011) demonstrated that a positive large-volume tap test (30-50 mL removal) with ≥10% improvement in TUG is a reliable predictor of shunt response. Sensitivity approximately 50-80%; specificity >75%.

Williams & Malm (2016) review in Continuum: DESH pattern and callosal angle <90° support iNPH diagnosis; amyloid PET may identify AD copathology (~50% of iNPH) and temper expectations for cognitive (but not gait) shunt benefit.
Marmarou et al. (2005) outline the diagnostic and management algorithm for iNPH including indications for VP shunt placement after positive tap testing and neurosurgical evaluation.

output.summary: Current evidence supports a standardized diagnostic pathway for probable iNPH: (1) clinical triad of gait disturbance, cognitive impairment, and urinary symptoms; (2) ventriculomegaly with Evans index >0.3 and DESH on MRI; (3) normal opening pressure on LP; (4) large-volume tap test (30-50 mL) with pre/post objective gait assessment as the primary shunt-response predictor. Literature also supports screening for AD copathology prior to shunting in cognitively impaired patients, and referral to neurosurgery when criteria are met.

background.pdr: 9-10 Hz posterior dominant rhythm, symmetric and reactive to eye opening
background.sleep_features: normal vertex waves and sleep spindles

eeg.impression: Normal awake and drowsy EEG. No epileptiform discharges and no electrographic seizures

findings: Normal sinus rhythm. Normal axis and intervals. No acute ST-T changes.

additional_observations: No acute intracranial haemorrhage, established infarct, mass, or midline shift.
Grey-white differentiation preserved; basal cisterns patent.
ct.impression: Non-contrast head CT without acute intracranial abnormality.

valves.mitral: mild annular calcification; no significant stenosis or regurgitation

findings: Mildly enlarged left atrium. Mild aortic valve sclerosis and mitral annular calcification without haemodynamic significance. No intracardiac thrombus or vegetation. No pericardial effusion. Grade I diastolic dysfunction, age-appropriate.
echo.impression: Preserved left ventricular systolic function. Mild left atrial enlargement and age-related valvular changes without haemodynamic significance

cardiac_monitoring.impression: Predominantly normal 24-hour Holter monitor with occasional isolated PACs. No significant arrhythmia detected.

general.summary: No directly applicable, high-quality evidence was retrieved for this query. Recommend correlating with current society guidelines.

differential.diagnosis: Vascular cognitive impairment / subcortical ischaemic vascular disease
differential.key_features: Mild white matter hyperintensity on MRI could suggest small-vessel disease; however, ventriculomegaly (Evans 0.36) is disproportionate to white matter burden, DESH is present, and a strongly positive tap test supports NPH over VCI as the primary diagnosis

Cognitive decline and family history of memory problems raise AD concern, but gait-predominant triad, DESH on MRI, normal CSF AD biomarkers, and frontal-subcortical (not amnestic) profile argue against AD as primary diagnosis
Shuffling gait and slowed movement overlap with parkinsonism; absence of resting tremor, cogwheel rigidity, and asymmetry, combined with magnetic gait and DESH pattern, favour iNPH

differential.diagnosis: Cerebral atrophy with secondary ex-vacuo ventriculomegaly
differential.key_features: Age-related atrophy could produce mild ventriculomegaly, but callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH pattern, and ventricular enlargement disproportionate to cortical sulcal atrophy argue against ex-vacuo dilation

differential.diagnosis: Cervical or lumbar spondylotic myelopathy/radiculopathy contributing to gait
differential.key_features: Age-related degenerative spine disease could contribute to gait difficulty; however, magnetic-pattern gait with freezing, frontal release signs, urinary urgency, and cognitive symptoms point to a central neurological syndrome rather than a primarily spinal mechanism

optimal_actions.action: Literature review of iNPH diagnostic criteria and shunt-response predictors
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Relkin 2005 INPH Study Group criteria (Evans >0.3, DESH, callosal angle <90°, normal opening pressure, tap test); Tisell 2011 tap-test sensitivity/specificity; Williams 2016 comprehensive review

optimal_actions.action: Brain MRI with measurement of Evans index and callosal angle, assessment of DESH pattern, and exclusion of mass effect, secondary hydrocephalus, and atrophy
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Ventriculomegaly with Evans index 0.36 (>0.3), callosal angle 72 degrees (<90°), DESH pattern, corpus callosum thinning, prominent aqueductal flow void, periventricular transependymal signal; mild white matter hyperintensity; no mass or obstructive lesion

optimal_actions.action: Reversible-cause labs (TSH, B12, RPR, HIV) to exclude metabolic and infectious dementia mimics
optimal_actions.expected_finding: TSH, B12, RPR, and HIV all normal; reversible causes of cognitive-gait syndrome excluded; mild hyperglycaemia consistent with known diabetes, not diagnostically relevant to triad

optimal_actions.action: Baseline neuropsychological battery to characterise cognitive profile and establish pre-tap reference for post-tap comparison
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Frontal-subcortical pattern: executive dysfunction and slowed processing predominate; episodic recognition relatively preserved relative to recall; language intact

optimal_actions.action: Large-volume lumbar puncture (40 mL tap test) with opening pressure measurement and pre/post objective gait and cognitive assessment
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Opening pressure 13 cmH2O (normal, <25 cmH2O); 40 mL removed; TUG improved 35% at 24 hours; 10-meter walk improved 32%; MoCA improved 3 points; CSF cytology, AD biomarkers normal

optimal_actions.action: Neurosurgery consultation for ventriculoperitoneal shunt candidacy evaluation and perioperative planning
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Neurosurgery accepts patient for VP shunt evaluation given positive imaging, clinical triad, and positive tap trial; programmable valve discussed

optimal_actions.action: Amyloid PET (optional) — assess for AD copathology that may reduce cognitive but not gait shunt benefit
optimal_actions.expected_finding: Negative amyloid PET (CL score 8) — AD copathology not identified; favourable prognosis for both gait and cognitive shunt response

useless_tools.rationale: EEG is non-specific for iNPH and does not contribute to diagnosis or differential from neurodegenerative alternatives in this chronic gait-cognitive-urinary triad
ECG is unrelated to the NPH diagnostic workup; no syncope, arrhythmia, or cardiogenic cause for symptoms is under consideration
Echocardiography has no role in iNPH evaluation in the absence of syncope or cardioembolic stroke workup
Head CT is inferior to MRI for measuring Evans index and callosal angle and for assessing DESH and periventricular signal; only justified if MRI is contraindicated
Cardiac monitoring has no diagnostic role in iNPH and is reserved for evaluation of syncope or arrhythmia

sequence_constraints.reason: Brain MRI must precede large-volume LP to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus before removing 30-50 mL of CSF, which could precipitate herniation if intracranial pressure is elevated from a mass
Baseline neuropsychological and gait assessment must be established before the tap test so that pre/post change can be quantified as the primary shunt-response predictor

critical_actions: Obtain brain MRI before lumbar puncture to exclude mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Establish objective pre-tap gait baseline (TUG and 10-metre walk) and neuropsychological baseline before performing the tap test
Remove 30-50 mL of CSF during the tap test; a low-volume LP is inadequate to test for shunt response
Reassess gait and cognition at 2 hours and 24 hours after the tap to capture the full tap-response window
Refer to neurosurgery for VP shunt evaluation when the full imaging, clinical, and tap-test criteria for iNPH are met
Recognise that the mild white matter changes on MRI are a distractor and do not account for the ventriculomegaly — DESH pattern and positive tap response confirm iNPH
contraindicated_actions: Do not perform large-volume lumbar puncture before MRI excludes mass effect or obstructive hydrocephalus
Do not attribute the full triad to 'small-vessel disease' on the basis of mild white matter hyperintensity alone when Evans index 0.36, DESH, and callosal angle 72 degrees are present
Do not diagnose iNPH on ventriculomegaly alone without confirming DESH pattern, callosal angle <90 degrees, normal opening pressure, and clinical triad
Do not attribute gait difficulty to diabetes, deconditioning, or age without completing the NPH diagnostic workup when the imaging and clinical picture is characteristic
key_reasoning_points: Classic iNPH (Relkin 2005) requires Hakim's triad with gait disturbance typically first and most prominent, chronic course >3-6 months, ventriculomegaly (Evans index >0.3) with DESH on MRI, normal opening pressure (<25 cmH2O), and exclusion of alternative diagnoses — all criteria met in this case

Evans index 0.36 and callosal angle 72 degrees are firmly in the diagnostic range for iNPH (threshold: Evans >0.3, callosal angle <90 degrees); the DESH pattern (narrow high-convexity sulci + widened Sylvian fissures) further supports the diagnosis

The mild periventricular and subcortical white matter hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2) is a common age-related finding and is disproportionately minor relative to the degree of ventriculomegaly — it does NOT explain the ventricular enlargement and does not refute the iNPH diagnosis

The large-volume tap test (40 mL, opening pressure 13 cmH2O) produced a clearly positive response: TUG improved 35% at 24 hours, 10-meter walk improved 32%, MoCA improved 3 points — consistent with shunt-responsive iNPH

Reversible mimics (hypothyroidism, B12 deficiency, syphilis, HIV) were excluded by normal TSH, B12, RPR, and HIV testing; AD copathology was not identified on CSF biomarkers (normal amyloid-42, tau, phospho-tau)

Frontal-subcortical neuropsychological profile (executive dysfunction and processing speed impairment predominating over episodic amnesia) with relative sparing of recognition memory and language is characteristic of iNPH rather than Alzheimer's disease

red_herrings.data_point: Mild-to-moderate periventricular and subcortical white matter T2/FLAIR hyperintensity (Fazekas grade 2) on brain MRI, with a prior CT 3 years ago noting 'minimal periventricular leukoaraiosis'
red_herrings.intended_effect: An agent anchoring on white matter disease may attribute the gait and cognitive symptoms primarily to small-vessel vascular disease (VCI) and deprioritise the NPH workup, especially noting the history of hypertension and diabetes
red_herrings.correct_interpretation: The white matter changes are mild (Fazekas grade 2), age-appropriate, and disproportionately minor relative to the degree of ventriculomegaly (Evans 0.36). The DESH pattern, callosal angle 72 degrees, and strongly positive tap test confirm iNPH as the primary diagnosis; mild white matter disease does not exclude NPH and does not account for the ventricular enlargement

metadata.difficulty_variant_description: Clean textbook straightforward iNPH in a 70-year-old woman — Evans 0.36, callosal angle 72 degrees, DESH, strongly positive tap trial (TUG +35%), full Hakim triad with gait most prominent. One grounded red herring: mild WMH that does not explain the ventriculomegaly. Distinguished from existing S cases by female sex, younger age, and diabetes comorbidity.

Classic Hakim triad, unambiguous imaging criteria, strongly positive tap response — straightforward despite the WMH distractor.
